title: Terumah: willing hearts (Exodus 25:2)
hook: the sanctuary is built only from gifts "of every man whose heart maketh him willing"

segments.voice: Yesterday Mishpatim ended with na'aseh v'nishma, we will do and we will hear. Your line was do, then understand. What did you try before you understood it? Today, a new portion, and a building project. Day three hundred fifty-three.

Think about the difference between two gifts. One is from a relative who was told by their spouse to send something, so a gift card arrives with a printed signature. The other is a mug from a child, lopsided, painted with way too much glue, handed to you with both hands. One cost more. You know which one you'll keep. God is about to ask the people to build a sanctuary in the wilderness, a dwelling place for the divine presence. It will need gold, silver, fabric, wood, oil. And the very first instruction is about where all of it is allowed to come from.
screen: `A GIFT CARD, A LOPSIDED MUG.` → `WHICH ONE DO YOU KEEP?` → `A SANCTUARY, AND WHERE IT COMES FROM.`

segments.voice: The portion is called Terumah, and it begins, in the old Jewish translation: "Speak unto the children of Israel, that they take for Me an offering; of every man whose heart maketh him willing ye shall take My offering." Terumah is the Hebrew word for that offering. Its root means to lift up, to raise. A terumah is something you lift out of what you have and set apart, the way you might lift the best piece onto someone else's plate. Then comes the list: gold, silver and copper; blue, purple and scarlet wool; fine linen and goats' hair; rams' skins dyed red; acacia wood; oil for the light; spices for the anointing oil and incense; onyx and other stones. Almost everything a people of former slaves might own, and some things they'd have to make. But notice the condition. Not a tax. Not a quota. Only from every person whose heart moves them. The Hebrew phrase is literally whose heart makes him willing, or urges him on. The rabbis noticed something else in the first line. It says take for me an offering, not give. Some Hasidic teachers liked to say that when you give from the heart, you're also taking: you receive something by giving. Whether or not you read it that way, the point of the opening is plain. A house for God built from forced gifts wouldn't be the house the Torah has in mind. It has to start with willing hearts.
screen: `THAT THEY TAKE FOR ME AN OFFERING.` · `TERUMAH: WHAT YOU LIFT UP.` · `GOLD, WOOL, WOOD, OIL, STONES.` · `WHOSE HEART MAKETH HIM WILLING.` · then, large: `ONLY WHAT'S WILLING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find what your heart wants to give. Settle, and breathe. Don't think about what you should give, or what's expected. Ask instead: what would I actually like to lift out of my life and offer? Some time. A skill. An object you no longer need that someone else would love. A compliment you've been holding back. Let something come up that feels light to give, not heavy. Notice the difference in your chest between should and want to. The bell holds the time.
Terumah. An offering, something lifted up and set apart. The name of the portion where the sanctuary is built only from willing hearts.
Your line: only what's willing. Today, give one thing freely, because you want to, not because you're asked. Day three hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: In Jewish life, giving is both a duty and a gift: tzedakah is expected of everyone, and alongside it Jews also give freely to synagogues and causes, often recalling that the sanctuary was built from gifts of willing hearts.

original.note: Hebrew: offering, from the root for raising up; the portion's name.

trapdoor: what you thought: a donation drive for a building.
what it means: a sanctuary that can only be built from what people want to give.
what a scholar hears: terumah, from the root r-w-m, to raise; the same word later names the priestly share lifted from the harvest.

notes: Exodus 25:2 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify exact wording and punctuation.
Materials list paraphrased from 25:3–7; 'rams' skins dyed red' and the skins often rendered 'sealskins' (tachash) omitted. Confirm list.
'Take, not give' reading is a common Hasidic and homiletic point; attributed generally. Keeper may give a source.
Terumah also names the priestly heave-offering from produce (Numbers 18); stated in the trapdoor.
